panels.description:
**WHAT** · slowest-5% response time. `p95` = 95% of requests finished faster than this; only the slowest 5% were worse. One ranked cut-off across all routes.

**READ** · <500ms green · <1s yellow · >1s red.

**INFER** · red + Saturation tile high → app is CPU / event-loop bound. Red + Saturation low → the DB or an outbound call is the cause. Buckets are pooled across pods first, then the cut-off taken — never an average of per-pod numbers.

Source: `http_server_duration_milliseconds_bucket`
panels.title: Latency p95

panels.description:
**WHAT** · error rate, split: HTTP = 5xx % of requests; Jobs = % of git-sync background jobs that errored.

**READ** · both 0 green. Either climbing = look at failing routes / failed jobs table.

targets.expr: (100 * (sum(rate(http_server_duration_milliseconds_count{job=~"$service", http_route!="/{*any}", http_route!="", http_status_code=~"5..",host_name=~"$host"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / clamp_min(sum(rate(http_server_duration_milliseconds_count{job=~"$service", http_route!="/{*any}", http_route!="",host_name=~"$host"}[$__range])), 0.001)) or vector(0)

panels.title: Errors

panels.description:
**WHAT** · total requests per second hitting the service.

**READ** · the trend matters more than the number. A sudden drop to near-zero = traffic is not reaching the app (load balancer, DNS, or routing problem). No colour — busy is normal.

**INFER** · compare against a normal day (shift the time picker back 1 day). Read it next to Saturation — high traffic with low Saturation = healthy headroom.

Source: `http_server_duration_milliseconds_count`
panels.title: Traffic

panels.description:
**WHAT** · how full Node's event loop is (its single work queue — while it is busy, nothing else runs). `0` = idle, `1` = no spare capacity. Live, refreshed every ~5s.

**READ** · <0.7 green · 0.7–0.85 yellow · >0.85 red.

**INFER** · the headline 'is Node overloaded' number. High = heavy JavaScript work, blocking I/O, or long garbage-collection pauses. When it is red, new requests wait in line.

Source: `nodejs_eventloop_utilization_ratio`
panels.title: Saturation

panels.description:
**WHAT** · errors in users' browsers (JS crashes + dead widgets) in the selected range.

**INFER** · backend Errors green but this red = the platform is fine, the *frontend* is broken — users see it, servers don't. Jump to the 🌍 Frontend section at the bottom.

**READ** · 0 green · ≥1 yellow · ≥20 red.
panels.title: Frontend errors

panels.description:
**WHAT** · `App` = the ToolJet build version · `Node` = the Node.js runtime version.

**READ** · `App: unknown` = the build did not stamp a version number. Two rows for one = a rollout in progress, pods still on different versions.

**INFER** · always check this first when triaging a bug — 'did it start after a deploy?'. A stuck two-version state means a rollout never finished.

Source: `service_version`, `process_runtime_version` labels
panels.title: Versions

panels.description:
**WHAT** · which deployment this dashboard is showing — e.g. `production`, `staging`.

**READ** · one word. Confirms you are looking at the environment you think you are.

**INFER** · sanity check before acting. Never debug prod on a staging dashboard, or vice-versa.

Source: `deployment_environment` label
panels.title: Environment

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Server = running app instances; Workers = WORKER=true pods consuming the BullMQ queues.

Source: nodejs_eventloop_utilization_ratio / bullmq_queue_workers
panels.title: Instances

panels.description:
**WHAT** · how many times the ToolJet process restarted inside the selected time range.

**READ** · `0` is what you want. Any non-zero = the app died and came back.

**INFER** · restarts mean crashes — usually an out-of-memory kill or an unhandled error. Pair with the Memory panel; if memory climbed to the limit just before a restart, it is an OOM. Repeated restarts = a crash loop.

Source: resets of `nodejs_eventloop_time_seconds_total`
panels.title: Restarts

panels.description:
**WHAT** · every route's RED numbers in one sortable table. RED = Rate (req/s), Errors (5xx %), Duration (latency). Range follows the time picker.

**COLUMNS** · req/s · p50 / p95 / p99 latency (p95 = 95% of requests were faster) · 5xx % · samples (how many requests — how trustworthy the row is).

**READ** · click any header to sort. High p95 = optimisation targets · high 5xx % = failing routes · high req/s = hot endpoints.

**INFER** · high p95 + low samples = too few requests to trust the number, ignore it. High p95 + high samples = a real bottleneck. Click a route name to drill into its latency.

Source: `http_server_duration_milliseconds_count` / `_bucket` by `http_route`

targets.expr: sum by (http_route) (rate(http_server_duration_milliseconds_sum{job=~"$service", http_route!="/{*any}", http_route!="",host_name=~"$host"}[$__range])) / sum by (http_route) (rate(http_server_duration_milliseconds_count{job=~"$service", http_route!="/{*any}", http_route!="",host_name=~"$host"}[$__range]))

panels.title: Route health

panels.description:
**WHAT** · service-wide latency over time at four cut-offs. `p50` = the typical request, `p99` = near-worst. A percentile is a ranked cut-off, not an average — one outlier cannot drag it.

**LINES** · p50 green · p90 yellow dashed · p95 orange · p99 red dotted.

**READ** · all four rising together = the whole service got slower. p99 rising while p50 stays flat = a slow tail, one rare slow path. A wide p50→p99 gap = inconsistent latency.

**INFER** · this answers 'is the service getting slower?'. Route health tells you which endpoint; this tells you whether to worry at all.

Source: `http_server_duration_milliseconds_bucket`
panels.title: Latency p50 / p90 / p95 / p99

panels.description:
**WHAT** · the full spread of response times over time. Each column = a time slice; brightness = how many requests landed in that latency band (bucket). Scoped by the `Route` filter at the top — `All` = whole service.

**READ** · one bright horizontal band = consistent latency. Two bright bands = two modes (e.g. fast cache hits + slow misses). A vertical bright streak = a brief spike.

**INFER** · shows shapes the percentile lines hide. If you see two bands, the 'p95' line is sitting in the empty gap between them and is misleading. Pick one route in the `Route` filter (or click a row in Route health) to drill into a single endpoint.

Source: `http_server_duration_milliseconds_bucket`
panels.title: Latency distribution heatmap

panels.description:
**WHAT** · requests per second split by response code, stacked.

**BANDS** · 2xx green = ok · 3xx blue = redirect · 4xx yellow = caller's fault · 5xx red = server's fault.

**READ** · red rising = server faults. Yellow rising = bad or unauthorised requests (login issues, or a scanner probing). Green dropping = traffic not arriving.

**INFER** · when red rises, open Failing routes (right) to see which endpoint is throwing.

Source: `http_server_duration_milliseconds_count` by `http_status_code`
panels.title: Status code rate

panels.description:
**WHAT** · only the routes that returned `4xx` or `5xx` in the time range, sorted worst-5xx first.

**COLUMNS** · 4xx = caller's-fault rejections · 5xx = server faults (red cell).

**READ** · top of the table = the most-failing route. A red 5xx cell is the one to act on.

**INFER** · fix 5xx first — that is the server breaking. 4xx on a known route = expired logins, stale clients, or someone scanning.

Source: `http_server_duration_milliseconds_count` by `http_route`, `http_status_code`
panels.title: Failing routes

panels.description:
**WHAT** · the slowest requests over 5 seconds. A trace = one request followed end-to-end; a span = one step inside it (a DB call, an HTTP call).

**READ** · each row = one slow request. Click the ▸ to see its spans inline.

**INFER** · click the Trace ID to open the full waterfall in Tempo — the request drawn as stacked timed bars, showing exactly which step ate the time.

Source: Tempo · `duration > 5s`
panels.title: Slow traces (>5s) · Tempo

panels.description:
**WHAT** · recent requests that failed (an error span anywhere inside). A trace = one request end-to-end; a span = one step inside it.

**READ** · each row = one failed request, newest on top. Click the ▸ to see the failed spans inline.

**INFER** · click the Trace ID for the full waterfall (the request as stacked timed bars) to see which step failed. Common: a DB call timing out, an outbound call returning 5xx, or an app exception.

Source: Tempo · `status = error`
panels.title: Recent error traces · Tempo

panels.description:
**WHAT** · requests that fired more than 25 database queries each. This is the classic N+1 problem (one request running many tiny queries in a loop instead of one).

**READ** · each row = one N+1-suspect request, longest first. Click the ▸ to see the repeated DB spans.

**INFER** · more round-trips = slower request, so duration ranks them. Open the Trace ID waterfall to see which query repeats — that is the loop to collapse into a single query.

Source: Tempo · postgres spans, `count() > 25`
panels.title: DB spans > 25

panels.description:
**WHAT** · individual database query spans that took over 5 seconds. A span = one DB call inside a request. Each row = ONE slow span (not the whole request).

**READ** · the Duration column is the SPAN duration (the actual slow query). Click ▸ — the SQL text is in the `db.statement` attribute. The trace ID jumps to the full waterfall.

**INFER** · the 'show me the actual slow query' panel. One genuinely slow query is rarer than N+1 (many fast queries) — that shows in 'DB spans > 25'.

Source: Tempo · postgres spans, `duration > 5s`
panels.title: Slow DB queries (>5s) · Tempo

options.content:
- Filters **App: Organization / Name / Environment / Context** scope this row only. Rows above are unaffected.
- Frontend data comes from a browser beacon batched every 30s (also on tab close). Expect ~90s lag. Errors are deduplicated, counts are true occurrences.
- Query panels are server-side counts (every run, edit + view). **App: Context** does not apply to them.
- Web-vitals panels honor org + context filters only (vitals carry no app/env labels).

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Total frontend errors (JS + widget) in the selected range, scoped by the App filters.

**INFER** · Rising with flat active users = a bug, not growth. Zero here with red panels below means the storm predates the range.

**READ** · Deduplicated client-side; counts are true occurrences. Click through to Loki via the data link for messages.
panels.title: Errors (range)

panels.description:
**WHAT** · sessions where the app never finished loading — an error or timeout hit before "app loaded" fired.

**INFER** · harder failure than a JS error: the user got a blank/stuck screen and never reached a usable app at all.

**READ** · 0 is normal. Any sustained count for one app/environment = that app is broken for entering users, not just a transient widget.
panels.title: App load failures

panels.description:
**WHAT** · registered users per workspace, broken out by role (admin/builder/end-user).

**INFER** · this is workspace-level headcount, not app-specific — it reflects who's registered, not who's active. Seats don't change when you switch apps.

**READ** · rising counts = growing workspace. Workspace-scope only — App: Name/Environment/Mode don't apply here, only App: Organization narrows this panel.
panels.title: Workspace seats

panels.description:
**WHAT** · distinct users who hit an app-scoped endpoint in the last 5 minutes, by role. A rolling gauge, not a running total — each point is its own 5-minute window.

**INFER** · plotted over time because the value only means anything against its own recent history. The dashboard time range is the x-axis here; it does not aggregate the number.

**READ** · a user working in two apps counts twice — this is per-app activity summed, not distinct humans. Compare against Workspace seats for registered headcount. App: Organization narrows this panel; App: Name/Environment/Context do not apply — the gauge comes from server-side API activity.
panels.title: Active users · 5-min window

panels.description:
**WHAT** · which apps have someone in them right now, same 5-minute window as the trend beside it.

**INFER** · answers "where is the activity", which is the question a single headline number always prompts next.

**READ** · apps whose name has not yet resolved are excluded, so a brand-new app can be missing for up to one seat-poll cycle (5 min).

defaults.noValue: Nobody active in the last 5 minutes

options.noValue: Nobody active in the last 5 minutes

targets.expr: topk(10, sum by (tooljet_app_name, tooljet_organization_name) (max by (tooljet_organization_id, tooljet_organization_name, tooljet_app_id, tooljet_app_name, tooljet_user_role) (tooljet_app_active_users{tooljet_app_name!="unknown", tooljet_organization_name=~"$app_org"}))) > 0

panels.title: Active users by app · now

panels.description:
**WHAT** · top 10 apps by combined js+widget error rate, scoped to the current filters.

**INFER** · this answers "is it just my app or everything" — one app dominating the topk = an app-specific bug; several apps rising together = a platform-wide regression.

**READ** · flat near zero per app is normal. A single app climbing = go investigate that app's recent changes/release.
panels.title: Errors/min by app

panels.description:
**WHAT** · p75 time from viewer mount to app fully loaded (line, left axis) with load failures per 5m (red bars, right axis).

**INFER** · Slow and broken belong together: rising p75 warns, bars mean users never saw the app at all — a load that never completes before the tab closes counts as a failure.

**READ** · Scoped by all App filters. Released-context failures are end-user facing — treat any bar as an incident signal.
panels.title: App load p75 + failures

panels.description:
**WHAT** · p75 of Google Web Vitals reported by real browser sessions.
- **lcp** (Largest Contentful Paint) — time until the main content is visible. Good ≤2.5s, poor >4s.
- **fcp** (First Contentful Paint) — time until anything renders. Good ≤1.8s.
- **ttfb** (Time To First Byte) — server+network time before HTML starts arriving. Good ≤0.8s.
- **inp** (Interaction to Next Paint) — worst-case lag between a click/keypress and the screen responding. Good ≤200ms, poor >500ms.
- **cls** (Cumulative Layout Shift, dashed, right axis) — unitless score of content jumping around. Good ≤0.1, poor >0.25.

**INFER** · Which metric is bad tells you where to look: high **ttfb** = backend/network, not frontend code. High **lcp/fcp** with normal ttfb = heavy bundles or slow initial render. High **inp** = main thread blocked — heavy JS, big tables re-rendering on every keystroke. High **cls** = widgets/images loading without reserved space, pushing content around.

**READ** · inp and cls only report when a tab is hidden/closed, so they trail live traffic. Vitals carry org+context labels only — App: Name/Environment filters do not apply here (no such labels on these metrics).
panels.title: Web vitals p75

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Most frequent frontend error fingerprints (message truncated to 80 chars) over the dashboard range, from Loki.

**INFER** · A single fingerprint dominating means one bug is hitting many users — fix that first. Many distinct low-count fingerprints suggest environment/network noise.

**READ** · Click a row’s data link to open matching raw errors in Explore. Counts are log-emit counts — storm-capped at 100/org/min, so metrics panels may show higher totals.

targets.expr: topk(20, sum by (tooljet_organization_name, error_fingerprint) (count_over_time({service_name="$service"} | event_type=~"js_error|widget_error" | tooljet_organization_name=~"$app_org" | tooljet_app_name=~"$app_name_var" | tooljet_environment_name=~"$app_env" | tooljet_app_context=~"$app_context" [$__range])))

panels.title: Top error messages

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Raw frontend error records (message = line) with app, widget and count context from Loki structured metadata.

**INFER** · This is the diagnosis pillar — expand a line to see the stacktrace (exception_stacktrace), org, user and fingerprint for any error spike seen in the metrics panels.

**READ** · Already deduplicated client-side (×N = occurrence count per browser flush). Retention: 14d.

targets.expr: {service_name="$service"} | event_type=~"js_error|widget_error" | tooljet_organization_name=~"$app_org" | tooljet_app_name=~"$app_name_var" | tooljet_environment_name=~"$app_env" | tooljet_app_context=~"$app_context" | line_format "{{if .tooljet_organization_name}}{{.tooljet_organization_name}} / {{end}}{{if .tooljet_app_name}}{{.tooljet_app_name}} · {{end}}{{if .tooljet_widget_type}}{{.tooljet_widget_type}} · {{end}}{{__line__}} ×{{.event_count}}"

panels.title: Recent frontend errors

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Query executions per minute (bars, left) and p95 query duration (line, right, ms) across the selected App scope.

**INFER** · Rising p95 with flat rate = data source slowdown. Rate cliff to zero on a busy app = queries failing before execution or app outage.

**READ** · Server-side, counts every query run (edit and view). App: Context filter does not apply here — use the app_mode label in ad-hoc queries for edit vs view.
panels.title: Queries/min + p95 latency

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Failed queries as a share of all query executions in the selected range, scoped by App filters.

**INFER** · The first true failure-percentage on this dashboard — a real denominator. >1% sustained = broken query or data source, not noise.

**READ** · No data = zero executions in range. 0% with errors elsewhere = frontend/widget errors, not query failures.
panels.title: Query failure %

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Query executions by data source kind (postgresql, restapi, runjs, …) in the selected range — top 10, scoped by App filters.

**INFER** · Shows what the apps actually lean on. A kind dominating here that also dominates Top failing queries = the integration to fix first.

**READ** · Kind = data source type, not SQL-vs-GUI — that lives in the query_type label.
panels.title: Top 10 query kinds (range)

panels.description:
**WHAT** · Queries with the most failures in the selected range: query name, app, data source kind, error type — scoped by App filters.

**INFER** · The work queue. One query dominating = fix that query. One error_type across many queries = data source or credentials problem.

**READ** · Empty = no failures in range (good). error_type is coarse (timeout / connection / permission / syntax / unknown).

defaults.noValue: No failed queries in this range

options.noValue: No query failures in this range

targets.expr: topk(20, sum by (tooljet_organization_name, tooljet_query_name, tooljet_app_name, tooljet_data_source_type, error_type) (increase(tooljet_query_executions_total{tooljet_organization_name=~"$app_org", tooljet_app_name=~"$app_name_var", tooljet_environment_name=~"$app_env", error_type!=""}[$__range]))) > 0

panels.title: Top failing queries (range)
Validation issues/min by code
panels.description:
**WHAT** · app validation issues per minute, by rule code and outcome (`blocked` = enforce rejected the write, `reported` = would block, returned as a warning, `warned` = warning).

**INFER** · a code climbing after a release = a new rule or a regression in whatever writes apps (builder, AI, import, API).

**READ** · split by `source` with Explore: `sum by (code, source) (rate(tooljet_app_validation_issues_total[5m]))`.

panels.title: Top validation issues (range)
panels.description:
**WHAT** · issue counts in the selected range by code, area, write source and outcome — top 20.

**INFER** · `source` says who wrote the bad app (builder, ai, import, pat …); `area` says which part of the app.

**READ** · `blocked` rows are writes users saw rejected; `reported`/`warned` rows went through with `validationWarnings`.

defaults.noValue: No validation issues in this range

targets.expr: topk(20, sum by (code, area, source, outcome) (increase(tooljet_app_validation_issues_total[$__range]))) > 0

panels.description:
`idle` = free. `used` = running query. `used peak` = max `used` in scrape window (catches short queries). `pending` = waiting for connection. `idle + used` = pool size.

`pending > 0` = pool exhausted. `used peak >> used` = sub-scrape bursts → see wait-time panel.
panels.title: DB pool · connections by state · pending requests

panels.description:
**WHAT** · how long database queries take, at three cut-offs (p50 typical, p95, p99 near-worst). All query types combined.

**READ** · the p99 line riding above p95 — the gap is the slow tail (one slow query type, or an occasional lock wait: a query stuck waiting for another to release a row).

**INFER** · HTTP latency rising but DB latency flat → the bottleneck is in app code, not the DB. Both rising together → the DB is the bottleneck.

Source: `db_client_operation_duration_seconds_bucket`
panels.title: DB op latency · p50 / p95 / p99

panels.description:
**WHAT** · database queries per second, split by database (`db_namespace` — e.g. the main app DB vs the metadata DB).

**READ** · compare this to Traffic (HTTP req/s). Queries-per-second ÷ requests-per-second ≈ DB calls per request.

**INFER** · more than ~10 DB calls per request = N+1 territory (a request looping tiny queries). Per-database lines show which schema each workload pressures.

Source: `db_client_operation_duration_seconds_count` by `db_namespace`
panels.title: DB op rate

panels.description:
**WHAT** · p95 latency (95% of queries faster than this) for each SQL operation type — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, COMMIT, and so on. Top 10.

**READ** · one line per operation. A rising SELECT line = slow reads. Rising UPDATE or COMMIT = slow writes or lock contention (queries waiting on each other).

**INFER** · this groups by operation kind, not by the exact SQL. For a specific slow query, use 'Slow DB queries' — that pulls the real SQL text from traces.

Source: `db_client_operation_duration_seconds_bucket` by `db_operation_name`
panels.title: DB latency by operation

panels.description:
**WHAT** · time a request waits to acquire a pool connection. p50 typical, p95 / p99 tail. Leading indicator — rises before `pending` shows on scrape snapshot.

**READ** · flat near 0 = pool keeps up. p95 climbing while pool state panel looks fine = checkouts are queuing in sub-scrape windows.

**INFER** · sustained p95 > query duration = pool saturated, raise `max` or fix slow queries. p99 spike with flat p50 = lock contention or transient burst.

Source: `db_client_connection_wait_time_seconds_bucket`
panels.title: DB pool · wait time to acquire connection · p50 / p95 / p99

panels.description:
**WHAT** · how busy Node's event loop is over time, per pod. The event loop is Node's single work queue — while it is busy, nothing else runs. `0` = idle, `1` = no spare capacity. One line per pod.

**READ** · above 0.7 sustained = saturation (requests will queue). Spikes line up with blocking work — large JSON parsing, synchronous file or crypto calls. Counter-rate source integrates active time over each window, so short bursts show up clearly (the gauge version misses them between samples).

**INFER** · the clearest 'Node is overloaded' signal — better than CPU%. One pod spiking while another stays flat = load-balancer imbalance.

Source: `nodejs_eventloop_time_seconds_total`, label `nodejs_eventloop_state = active`
panels.title: Event-loop utilization

panels.description:
**WHAT** · CPU used by the ToolJet process only, measured in cores (`1.0` = one full CPU core fully used).

**STATES** · `user` = running JavaScript / app code · `system` = the kernel doing work for the app (network, disk, system calls).

**READ** · this is the app alone — compare it with Host CPU (the whole machine). Sustained high `system` = lots of I/O or system calls.

**INFER** · app CPU and event-loop utilization rising together = the app itself is compute-bound. App CPU low but Host CPU high = a neighbour process (Postgres, a sidecar) is eating the machine.

Source: `process_cpu_time_seconds_total` by `process_cpu_state`
panels.title: App CPU · cores by state

panels.description:
**WHAT** · the app's memory over time. `RSS` = total memory the process holds in RAM (JavaScript objects + buffers + native). `V8 heap used` = memory for JavaScript objects. `V8 heap limit` = the configured ceiling for that heap.

**READ** · the gap between RSS and heap-used = native and buffer memory.

**INFER** · V8 heap used climbing toward the limit and never dropping = a JavaScript memory leak → expect a crash / restart. RSS growing while heap stays flat = a native or buffer leak (rarer).

Source: `process_memory_usage`, `v8js_memory_heap_used_bytes`, `v8js_memory_heap_limit_bytes`
panels.title: Memory · RSS · V8 heap used · V8 heap limit

panels.description:
**WHAT** · the JavaScript heap broken into V8's internal regions. `new_space` = freshly created short-lived objects · `old_space` = objects that survived long enough to be promoted · `code_space` = compiled (JIT) code.

**READ** · `new_space` is small and churns fast · `old_space` is the bulk and should rise then fall as GC reclaims it.

**INFER** · `old_space` climbing steadily and never falling back = a leak: objects kept alive by mistake. Big `new_space` spikes = a hot path allocating heavily.

Source: `v8js_memory_heap_used_bytes` by `v8js_heap_space_name`
panels.title: V8 heap by space · used bytes

panels.description:
**WHAT** · how long the app froze for garbage collection (GC = Node automatically freeing unused memory; the app pauses while it runs). Shown by GC type.

**KINDS** · `scavenge` (minor) — fast cleanup of short-lived objects, usually under 1ms · `mark-sweep-compact` (major) — slow full-heap sweep, can be tens of ms · `incremental` — a major GC chopped into small slices so it never freezes the app for long in one go · `weak` — clears weak references, tiny.

**READ** · p99 = the worst 1% of pauses. Major-GC p99 over 50ms = users feel a stutter.

**INFER** · major GC pauses growing = the heap is under pressure → raise the heap limit or allocate less. Lots of incremental GC = V8 working hard to avoid one big freeze — still a pressure signal.

**CAVEAT** · this histogram caps at 100 ms (default OTel bucket boundaries). Pauses longer than 100 ms get reported AS 100 ms — so a `p99 ≈ 100 ms` line probably hides bigger real pauses. Code-side fix is to extend the histogram buckets via an OTel `View` at MeterProvider setup; same fix the HTTP latency histogram needs.

Source: `v8js_gc_duration_seconds_bucket` by `v8js_gc_type`
panels.title: GC pause duration · p50 / p95 / p99 by kind

panels.description:
**WHAT** · CPU use of the whole machine (every process), averaged across all cores, by category. `idle` is removed so the stack height = real usage.

**STATES** · `user` = application code · `system` = kernel work · `iowait` = cores stalled waiting for disk · `nice` / `softirq` / `steal` = small contributors (`steal` = CPU taken by the cloud host).

**READ** · y-axis fixed 0–100%; the empty gap above the stack is spare capacity. High `user` = compute-bound · high `system` = system-call heavy · high `iowait` = disk-bound.

**INFER** · separates 'the app is busy' from 'the machine is busy on kernel / disk work'. Pair with event-loop utilization — high CPU + high loop = the app itself.

Source: `system_cpu_utilization` by `system_cpu_state`
panels.title: Host CPU in use · by state

panels.description:
**WHAT** · physical RAM of the Kubernetes node (the whole VM) — NOT the pod. `used` (orange fill) vs `total RAM` (grey dashed ceiling).

**WHY ~31 GiB, not 16** · metrics read from inside a container still report the underlying node, not the pod's own cap. This node (~31 GiB) runs ~2 ToolJet pods, each capped at 16 GiB. The per-pod cap is not scraped here.

**READ** · orange fill = every process on the node · the gap up to the dashed line = node headroom · averaged across pods (both observe the same node).

**INFER** · this is node-level pressure. For the ToolJet process's own memory use the Node.js 'Memory' panel.

Source: `system_memory_usage` by `system_memory_state`
panels.title: Node memory · used vs total

panels.description:
**WHAT** · network traffic of the machine, split by direction — received vs transmitted bytes per second, across all interfaces.

**READ** · spikes line up with traffic surges, file uploads, or noisy clients. A rate sitting near the network card's line speed = the link is saturated.

**INFER** · read it next to HTTP req/s. Network climbing without matching HTTP load = something else on the wire — log shipping, DB replication, backups.

Source: `system_network_io_total` by `network_io_direction`
panels.title: Host network IO · rx/tx bytes/sec

panels.description:
**WHAT** · bad network packets per second. `dropped` = packets the kernel threw away (buffers full, backpressure). `errors` = hardware-level faults (bad frames, faulty cable or driver).

**READ** · any sustained non-zero rate is abnormal — a healthy machine sits flat at zero.

**INFER** · drop spikes lining up with HTTP 5xx = client connections cut before the app could reply. Errors without drops = a hardware or driver fault, not load.

Source: `system_network_dropped_total`, `system_network_errors_total`
panels.title: Host network errors · drops + errors/sec

panels.description:
**WHAT** · p95 latency (95% of calls faster than this) of HTTP calls ToolJet makes OUT to other services — Git providers, login providers, the plugin marketplace, S3. Top 8.

**READ** · one line per upstream host. A spike = that dependency slowed down.

**INFER** · if user-facing latency rose and one outbound host's p95 rose at the same time, that host is dragging requests. Common: GitHub rate limits, a slow login provider, a marketplace timeout.

Source: `http_client_duration_milliseconds_bucket` by `net_peer_name`
panels.title: Outbound HTTP p95 by host

panels.description:
**WHAT** · outbound calls per second, split by destination host and response code.

**READ** · a rate spike to one host = a retry storm or a new feature. Mixed 4xx / 5xx = that upstream is returning errors.

**INFER** · pair with the p95 panel. High rate + high p95 = you are overloading that upstream. High rate + low p95 = it is coping. High p95 + flat rate = it slowed down on its own.

Source: `http_client_duration_milliseconds_count` by `net_peer_name`, `http_status_code`
panels.title: Outbound HTTP rate by host & status

panels.description:
**WHAT** · outbound calls per second by response code, stacked. These are calls ToolJet makes OUT to other services.

**BANDS** · 2xx green = ok · 3xx blue = redirect · 4xx yellow = upstream rejected us (bad auth, rate limit) · 5xx red = upstream is faulting.

**READ** · yellow rising = a dependency is rejecting us (expired token, quota hit). Red rising = an upstream is down or degraded.

**INFER** · pair with 'Outbound HTTP p95 by host' — errors and latency on the same host together = that upstream is the problem.

Source: `http_client_duration_milliseconds_count` by `http_status_code`
